interactions.summary: A student proposes that Piccarda failed to exercise free will, while Jiang pushes back that armed coercion collapses easy talk about simply refusing and forces the class into extreme scenarios like escape or death.
The class introduces the Catholic ban on suicide, and Jiang seizes it as the crucial constraint for understanding why death cannot be treated as the obvious path of resistance.

Jiang explains a Christian body-soul distinction through Augustine and then returns the class to the unresolved question of why Piccarda remains in the lower sphere if bodily violation should not matter.

speaker_notes.note: The student segment is partially garbled, but it functions as a prompt about why raped Christian women would consider suicide before Jiang supplies the doctrinal answer.

claims.claim: Jiang rejects the idea that Piccarda's free will could be straightforwardly exercised by simple refusal because the scene involves literal armed force dragging her away.
Jiang says that in medieval Catholicism suicide is treated as the worst sin, and he presents that doctrine as the reason self-killing cannot solve the forced-marriage paradox.
Jiang explains the anti-suicide doctrine by saying many raped women once killed themselves to go directly to Jesus, prompting the church to insist that self-killing is forbidden.
Jiang invokes Augustine to argue that bodily violation matters less than the state of the soul: the body belongs to earth, while the soul belongs to God.
Jiang turns that doctrine back into the paradox by asking why Piccarda is still in the lower sphere if bodily rape or forced marriage should not matter and faith is what counts.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang calls suicide the worst sin in the world, making death an unusable escape hatch inside the moral system under discussion.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the worst sin in the world is suicide
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It names the hard doctrinal constraint that prevents the class from solving the paradox by martyr-style self-destruction.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang divides body and soul so sharply that rape and forced marriage become earthly injuries while the soul remains God's concern.
signature_moments.source_phrase: your body belongs to this earth ... your soul belongs to god
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's strongest formulation of the theological frame that Piccarda's case is supposed to inhabit.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's summary of the medieval Catholic prohibition that closes off self-killing as a legitimate answer to coercion.
The Christian authority Jiang cites for the claim that protecting the soul matters more than preserving the body from violation.
The doctrine Jiang uses to argue that worldly violence cannot touch the soul's fidelity to God.

chronology_notes.note: This June 15 packet deepens the Piccarda paradox by adding the medieval Catholic ban on suicide and Augustine's body-soul distinction, which still fail to explain the lower-sphere placement.

uncertainty_notes.note: The ASR drops part of the transition from raped women to Augustine, so the extraction keeps the stable doctrinal contrast between bodily violation and the soul's relation to God.
